stem: A nurse compares C-reactive protein (CRP) with erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) for monitoring an inflammatory process. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: CRP generally rises and falls more rapidly with changes in inflammatory activity, whereas ESR usually responds more slowly and may remain elevated longer.
options.B: CRP is disease-specific, whereas ESR identifies the exact inflammatory diagnosis whenever either marker becomes elevated above its reference range.
options.C: ESR typically rises within several hours and returns to baseline promptly, while CRP usually remains unchanged during acute inflammatory activity.
options.D: CRP and ESR are unaffected by inflammatory activity, so serial changes in either test do not contribute useful information about an inflammatory process.

rationale: NCBI/StatPearls describes CRP and ESR as nonspecific inflammatory markers with different response kinetics. CRP begins to rise within roughly 4–6 hours and changes rapidly with inflammatory stimuli, declining promptly as the trigger resolves. ESR generally begins to rise after about 24–48 hours and can remain elevated longer because it indirectly reflects changes in acute-phase proteins and red-cell aggregation. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly makes the tests disease-specific, C reverses their response kinetics, and D incorrectly denies their relationship to inflammation.
educational_objective: Differentiate the response kinetics of CRP and ESR and recognize that both are nonspecific inflammatory markers.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls)
source_document_title: Physiology, Acute Phase Reactants; C-Reactive Protein: Clinical Relevance and Interpretation; Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
source_version_date: Current StatPearls 2026 edition; ESR last update July 7, 2025; live NCBI pages retrieved 2026-08-26
source_locator: Acute Phase Reactants: ESR starts to rise within 24–48 h; CRP starts after 4–6 h. CRP Clinical Relevance: unlike ESR, CRP changes rapidly and declines promptly after trigger resolution. ESR: nonspecific inflammatory test interpreted with other diagnostics.
source_claim_supported: CRP generally responds to inflammatory change more rapidly than ESR, while both markers are nonspecific.

audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — current NCBI sources directly establish faster CRP kinetics and slower ESR response; A uniquely matches.
